hops.afterHeading: The signature: a threshold that falls and stays down
hops.title: Horsehair on a glass rod
hops.text: Pinch a loose strand of your own hair near its middle and press the tip straight down on the back of your hand until it bends. Now slide your fingers closer to the tip and try again: the shorter length takes a firmer push before it bows. In 1894 Maximilian von Frey put that to work, attaching horsehairs of different lengths to glass rods to test how sensitive the cornea was. Longer hairs bent under a feather-light press; shorter ones pushed harder. In 1955 Boberg-Ans switched his corneal tester to nylon, and labs still press calibrated nylon filaments against a rodent's paw to find its withdrawal threshold.

sources.citation: Crabtree et al., "Corneal nerve assessment by aesthesiometry: history, advancements, and future directions," Vision 2024 (PMC11130793)
Vincenot et al., "A 5000-year overview of the history of pain," Pain Reports 2025 (PMC11970827)
Deuis, Dvorakova and Vetter, "Methods used to evaluate pain behaviors in rodents," Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience 2017

image.caption: Shorter hairs need more force to bend, the idea behind von Frey filaments, first made from horsehair in 1894.

hops.afterHeading: The ganglion that will not stop firing
hops.title: The made-up soldier who got real donations
hops.text: In July 1866, The Atlantic Monthly ran an unsigned story about George Dedlow, a Civil War soldier who lost both arms and both legs yet still felt his missing limbs. Its author, neurologist Silas Weir Mitchell, built Dedlow from injuries he saw in real soldiers, and he later recalled that kind readers collected money for Dedlow and went to Philadelphia's "Stump Hospital" to visit. In 2014, Vaso and colleagues used lidocaine to block the spinal roots, the dorsal root ganglia or both in 31 people with leg amputations. Phantom pain eased quickly, which led the authors to argue that it is driven mainly by activity in the ganglion.

sources.citation: Center for the History of Medicine, Countway Library, Harvard Medical School: "The Case of George Dedlow" (OnView item 6104)
Vaso et al., "Peripheral nervous system origin of phantom limb pain," Pain 2014 (PMID 24769187)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An old writing desk with an oil lamp, a quill in an inkwell, blank pages, a soldier's blue cap and a small purse of coins.
image.caption: Mitchell's 1866 story made phantom limbs famous; a 2014 study suggests the pain can start in the ganglion.

hops.afterHeading: The twist: the chain depends on sex and compartment
hops.title: The myth that female mice give messier data
hops.text: For decades, many labs tested only male animals on a confident hunch: female hormone cycles would make the data too messy to trust. Counting 2009 animal studies in four neuroscience journals, Beery and Zucker found about five male-only studies for every female-only one. Then Prendergast, Onishi and Zucker pooled 293 mouse articles and checked the hunch. Female mice whose cycles nobody tracked were not significantly more variable than males on any trait, and males were substantially more variable on several. So the noise excuse did not hold up. When Sorge, Mapplebeck and colleagues tested both sexes after a nerve injury, female mice took a different immune route to touch hypersensitivity.

sources.citation: Beery and Zucker, "Sex bias in neuroscience and biomedical research," Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 2011 (PMID 20620164)
Sorge, Mapplebeck et al., "Different immune cells mediate mechanical pain hypersensitivity in male and female mice," Nature Neuroscience 2015 (PMC4772157)
Prendergast, Onishi and Zucker, "Female mice liberated for inclusion in neuroscience and biomedical research," Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 2014 (PMID 24456941)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two white mice, one in each pan of a level brass balance, beside a blank notebook and reading glasses on a lab bench.
image.caption: Across 293 mouse articles, female mice were not significantly more variable than males.
